facts.statement: Palaeocarcharias is an extinct genus of shark found in Europe during the Jurassic period.
facts.quote: Palaeocarcharias is an extinct genus of shark, known from the Jurassic of Europe.

facts.statement: Isolated teeth from England suggest the genus Palaeocarcharias existed back to the Middle Jurassic (Bathonian).
facts.quote: Isolated teeth of indeterminate species from England (White Limestone Formation, and possibly the Forest Marble and Taynton Limestone) extend the range of the genus back to the Middle Jurassic (Bathonian).

facts.statement: Palaeocarcharias resembled carpet sharks and reached a total body length of about 1 meter.
facts.quote: Morphologically, it closely resembles carpet sharks (Orectolobiformes), and is around 1 m in total body length.

facts.statement: A 2018 study proposed classifying it as the sole member of the order Palaeocarchariiformes, while a 2023 study favored placing it within Lamniformes.
facts.quote: A 2018 study suggested that should be classified as the sole member of the order Palaeocarchariiformes, but a subsequent 2023 study questioned this and favoured placement in Lamniformes.

facts.statement: A 2024 study suggested that a specimen from Canjuers might actually be a true carpet shark belonging to Orectolobidae.
facts.quote: A 2024 study of a specimen from Canjuers suggested that as that it was in fact a true carpet shark, perhaps a member of Orectolobidae (the wobbegongs).

facts.statement: The Paleobi Database lists the parent group of Palaeocarcharias as Lamniformes.
The genus lived from the Bathonian to the Tithonian, between 168.2 and 145.06 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Bathonian to Tithonian (168.2 to 145.06 million years ago)

rejected.statement: The only named species, Palaeocarcharias stromeri, is known from exceptionally preserved fossils in the Late Jurassic (Tithonian) of Germany and France.
rejected.quote: It has only a single named species, Palaeocarcharias stromeri, which is known from exceptionally preserved specimens from the Late Jurassic (Tithonian) of Germany (Solnhofen Limestone) and France (Canjuers Lagerstatte).

rejected.quote: However, it shares greater similarities in tooth development with mackerel sharks (Lamniformes), including the absence of orthodentine.
